name: Apache Spark
summary: The general-purpose distributed engine for large batch jobs, streaming and machine learning, in Python, SQL, Scala, Java or R.
intro: A Spark application has a driver, which turns your DataFrame code or SQL into a plan of stages, and executors, which run each stage as many parallel tasks, one per partition of the data. Between stages, data is shuffled across the network, and it spills to disk when it doesn’t fit in memory, so a job can process far more data than the cluster has RAM. If an executor dies, Spark recomputes the partitions it lost. The same engine runs batch jobs, Structured Streaming and MLlib.

Spark runs on Kubernetes, YARN or its own standalone cluster manager, and as managed services such as Databricks, Amazon EMR, AWS Glue and Google Cloud’s Managed Service for Apache Spark (formerly Dataproc). Table formats plug in as libraries: Iceberg, Delta Lake and Hudi each ship a Spark runtime. Spark 4.0 (May 2025) made ANSI SQL mode the default, added a `VARIANT` type for semi-structured data and moved to Java 17 and Scala 2.13. Spark Connect lets thin clients, including a 1.5 MB Python client, use a remote cluster. The current release is 4.2.0, from July 2026.
strengths: One engine for ETL, SQL, streaming and machine learning
Scales from a laptop to clusters of thousands of nodes, and recomputes lost partitions when an executor fails
Iceberg, Delta Lake and Hudi each ship a Spark integration that reads and writes their tables
Managed services on every major cloud, such as Amazon EMR, Google Cloud’s Managed Service for Apache Spark (formerly Dataproc) and Databricks
limits: Built for clusters: each application starts its own driver and executor processes before any work begins
Tuning shuffles, partition counts and memory is a skill of its own; skewed keys cause stragglers and out-of-memory errors
Spark 4 dropped Java 8 and 11 and Scala 2.12, so upgrading from 3.x means dependency work

story: By 2009, Hadoop MapReduce was the standard way to process big data on a cluster, but it had one habit that hurt: every job read its input from disk and wrote its output back. Machine learning algorithms that pass over the same data dozens of times reloaded it on every pass, and an analyst running ad-hoc queries through Hive or Pig waited tens of seconds for each one, because each query was a separate MapReduce job.

Spark was created that year in UC Berkeley’s AMPLab by Matei Zaharia, working with Ion Stoica, Scott Shenker and others. The idea was to keep a working set of data in memory across many parallel operations while keeping MapReduce’s scalability and fault tolerance. The first paper, at HotCloud 2010, reported Spark running iterative machine learning 10x faster than Hadoop and scanning a 39 GB dataset interactively with sub-second latency. The code was released under a BSD licence in 2010, the 2012 NSDI paper on Resilient Distributed Datasets won Best Paper, and in 2013 the creators founded Databricks and moved Spark to Apache.
Libraries for SQL, streaming, machine learning and graphs grew on top of the same core.

choices.choice: Keep data in memory between steps
choices.why: Iterative algorithms and repeated queries spent most of their time rereading the same input from disk. Caching a dataset in RAM across a cluster removed that cost for multi-pass work.

choices.choice: Recover lost data from lineage, not replicas
choices.why: Replicating every in-memory dataset would double memory use and network traffic. An RDD instead remembers the coarse transformations (`map`, `join`, `groupBy`) that built it, so Spark can recompute just a lost partition.

choices.choice: Written in Scala, usable from an interactive shell
choices.why: Scala ran on the JVM next to Hadoop but offered functional operations and closures that could be shipped to workers. A modified Scala interpreter let users explore large datasets on a cluster interactively.

choices.choice: One engine for batch, SQL, streaming and ML
choices.why: Instead of separate systems for each workload, Shark (later Spark SQL), Spark Streaming, MLlib and GraphX were built on the same execution core, so data didn’t have to move between systems.
